extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (patent prosecutors and applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim language is definite under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph), covering terms of degree, relative references, approximations, numerical ranges, antecedent basis, functional language, and other claim-drafting issues that can render claims indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of degree must be understandable in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the specification uses the same term of degree as the claim, a rejection is proper if the scope of the term is not understood when read in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the scope is unclear, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112, second paragraph). Broadening modifiers are common drafting tools but do not excuse unclear scope (see In re Wiggins). Examiners should ensure the metes and bounds are discernible from the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object may render a claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite when a limitation is defined by reference to an object and the relationship between the limitation and the object is not sufficiently defined, leading to two or more plausible constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine if the examiner can readily ascertain positional or relational relationships of elements (see Ex parte Miyazaki and Ex parte Brummer). If relationships lack a known standard or rely on an unspecified object (e.g., rider of unspecified build), the claim may be indefinite. Conversely, references that are as accurate as the subject permits (e.g., 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats') may be definite (Orthokinetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'about' and other approximations must be evaluated in context
rubrics_metrics.description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' (and similar approximations) must be determined by considering the context in the specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual factors and available measurement techniques matter (e.g., W.L. Gore holding 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite because it was measurable). However, 'at least about' can be indefinite in presence of close prior art and no guidance from spec or prosecution (Amgen). Examiners should look for intrinsic or extrinsic indicators of the intended tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'essentially' depends on disclosure providing an objective line
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'essentially' can be definite if the specification supplies guidelines and examples enabling a POSITA to distinguish unavoidable impurities from essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification gives sufficient guidance (e.g., In re Marosi regarding 'essentially free of alkali metal'), the phrase is acceptable; applicants are not required to state precise numeric cutoffs when impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'similar' can be indefinite if scope unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitations using 'similar' (e.g., 'similar apparatus' or 'similar structure') may be indefinite because it may be unclear what the applicant intends to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Kristensen and Ex parte Pappas show such recitations were held indefinite. Examiners should assess whether the specification clarifies the intended scope of 'similar.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'substantially' is broad but can be definite with guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantially' is a broad term often used with other terms to describe characteristics; it can be definite if the specification contains guidelines that allow a POSITA to understand the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Nehrenberg, In re Mattison, Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics) shows claims with 'substantially' were held definite where the disclosure provided an objective basis. Examiners should look for such guidelines in the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of 'type' to otherwise definite expressions may render them indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the word 'type' (e.g., 'Friedel-Crafts catalyst type', 'ZSM-5-type') can extend scope and make the claim indefinite if it is unclear what 'type' is intended to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig) demonstrate that 'type' can create ambiguity, especially when dependent claims include species not clearly within the genus. Examiners should evaluate whether the term 'type' creates unclear boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective terms require objective standards in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim uses a subjective term, the examiner must determine whether the specification supplies an objective standard for measuring scope; without such an objective standard, the claim may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims depending solely on unrestrained subjective opinions (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing' in Datamize) are indefinite. Applicants may overcome rejections by amending to remove the subjective term or by providing evidence/guidance showing how a POSITA would ascertain the term's meaning. Note: providing mere examples may not always satisfy the requirement (DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific numerical ranges generally do not raise definiteness issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim generally does not raise an issue of indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, context matters—see additional rules for mixing ranges, open-ended ranges, and 'effective amount' limitations. Examiners should still confirm that the ranges have discernible boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim may render the claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Including both a narrow range and a broader range within a single claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries are not discernible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples like 'a temperature between 45 and 78 °C, preferably between 50 and 60 °C' have been held indefinite when placed in a single claim. Preferential or example-based narrower ranges belong in the specification, a dependent claim, or a separate independent claim. Dependent claims setting narrower ranges than their parent are acceptable (e.g., 70-150 ohms and dependent 70-100 ohms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended numerical ranges should be carefully analyzed
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') can create ambiguities depending on how they interact with other claim recitations, composition bases, or dependent claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether other claim language inadvertently excludes the open-ended component (e.g., percentages adding to 100%). Court decisions (In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch) show claims may be held definite even if theoretically impossible combinations are included. Terms like 'up to' can include zero (In re Mochel); 'not more than 70% by weight' may read on dry material (Ex parte Khusid).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Effective amount' may or may not be indefinite depending on disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 'an effective amount' is definite turns on whether a person skilled in the art could determine specific values from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification provides guidance or examples enabling POSITA to determine effective values and the amount is not critical, the phrase may be definite (In re Mattison; In re Halleck). It can be indefinite if the claim fails to state the function to be achieved or more than one effect is implied (In re Fredericksen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary claim language ('for example', 'such as') can create ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using language that purports to list examples or preferences in claims may lead to confusion about whether the examples are limiting, and thus may render the claim indefinite in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not automatically make a claim indefinite, but examples exist where such phrasing was held indefinite (see listed historical Ex parte cases). Examiners should analyze whether the example language makes the intended scope unclear. See MPEP § 2173.02 for when a 112(b) rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear due to lack of antecedent basis (e.g., referencing 'said lever' when no lever was previously recited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess antecdent basis (In re Packard). However, lack of explicit antecedent basis does not always make a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by POSITA (Ex parte Porter). Inherent characteristics can provide antecedent basis (Bose v. JBL). Examiners should suggest corrections for antecedent problems where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms in the claim body not recited in the preamble are not per se indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of elements from the claim preamble does not automatically render a claim indefinite; the totality of claim limitations and their interaction determine definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the whole claim to ascertain the inventor's contribution and whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope. See In re Larsen where an omitted preamble element did not make the claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to limitations in another claim is acceptable if not confusing
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a preceding claim to define a limitation (e.g., 'The product produced by the method of claim 1') is acceptable and not necessarily indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such references are proper unless the format of the reference results in confusion. Examiners should also check compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA 112, fourth paragraph) when examining dependent claims (see MPEP § 608.01(n), subsection III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations are permissible but must convey clear scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language (defining a feature by what it does rather than by what it is) is not inherently improper; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) permits means-plus-function claiming, and functional language may be used outside that format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate functional limitations for what they fairly convey to POSITA in context. Functional language that pairs structure with function (e.g., conical spout that 'allow[s] several kernels' as in In re Schreiber) may be acceptable. Purely result-oriented or problem-statement functional language can be indefinite because it fails to limit scope and may encompass all means of achieving the result (Halliburton; Ariad; Hyatt). Unlimited functional claims may also raise written description/enablement issues (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Be mindful of the difference between general descriptive terms and means-plus-function treatment (Phillips v. AWH; K-2 Corp.).
